title: One stop of light
subtitle: A field guide to shutter speed and exposure
creator: Palim
description: Choose a shutter speed, understand the light you trade, and test the result in three frames.

chapters.title: Choose what moves
chapters.markdown:
A cyclist crosses a patch of evening light. You want a sharp rider against a quiet background. Start with the movement: how much blur belongs in this picture?

**Shutter speed is exposure time.** At 1/500 second, the shutter is open for half as long as at 1/250. A moving subject has less time to travel across the image, so a shorter exposure can reduce motion blur. No single setting guarantees a sharp photograph.

## Halve the time, halve the light

Keep the scene and lens opening fixed. If 1/500 second admits one unit of light, 1/250 admits two and 1/125 admits four. These are calculated ratios, not camera measurements.

![Light admitted at three shutter times](figure:shutter-times)

The bars describe light, not sharpness. Motion blur also depends on how the subject and camera move. Choose the effect you want first; then account for the light that choice gives up.

> A faster shutter gives motion less time. It also gives light less time.

chapters.title: Exchange one stop
chapters.markdown:
Your starting exposure is **f/8 at 1/250 second, ISO 200**. You choose 1/500 for the rider. The time halves: you have given up one stop of light.

Open the lens from f/8 to f/5.6 to gain approximately one stop in return. The smaller f-number means a larger opening. With the scene and ISO unchanged, these two settings can give a similar brightness.

![An opening and exposure time, compared](figure:light-path)

## Equal light, different picture

The exchange changes more than brightness. The faster shutter can reduce motion blur; the wider lens opening can make less of the scene appear in focus. Decide whether that trade suits your picture.

If the lens cannot open further, increasing ISO may give a useful image brightness. It does not put back the light lost by shortening the exposure.

> One stop means twice as much light, or half as much. It does not mean the same photograph.

chapters.title: Make three frames
chapters.markdown:
Find a subject moving across your view, such as leaves in the wind. Work from a safe, steady position and keep your framing and the light as consistent as possible.

Select shutter-priority mode. Turn Auto ISO off and keep ISO fixed: you want to see the camera change the aperture, without ISO changing too.

1. Make a frame at **1/125 second**. Note the aperture the camera chooses.
2. Repeat at **1/250**, then **1/500**. Note each aperture and any exposure warning.
3. Compare the same moving edge in all three frames, at the same magnification.

## Look before you judge

Choose the frame that shows the movement you wanted. Then check what changed:

- **Moving edges:** did the shorter exposure reduce the blur?
- **Background:** did the changing aperture affect what appears in focus?
- **Brightness:** if a frame is darker, did the lens reach its widest opening?

If the light changed or the subject moved differently, repeat the set before drawing a conclusion. This is an observation of your scene, not a universal camera setting.

Write one field note: “I chose ___ because ___. The camera changed ___.”

> Choose the effect. Change one setting. Notice the trade.
